I'm 65 years old and I've farmed these fields in Quzhou my whole life. I only went to primary school, but I know this land better than any book. My sons work in Handan city now, so it's just me and my wife managing the plots. I don't have the back for experimenting anymore, and I won't gamble on crops that need chasing buyers.

This year, like every year, I'll put my 4 mu into the wheat-maize rotation. It's the only system that makes sense here on the North China Plain. Come October, after the autumn rains soften the soil, I'll run the rotary tiller and sow winter wheat. I'll buy improved seed from the village supply store — a reliable variety like Shimai or Lumai. I've learned you can't skip fertilizer if you want a decent harvest, so I'll spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. Water is everything here; our wells aren't as deep as they used to be, so I'll irrigate three times — once before winter freeze, and twice in spring. I'll spray herbicide once, and keep an eye out for aphids and rust — usually two more sprays handles it. If the weather treats me fair, I should get about 1000 jin per mu.

The day I harvest that wheat in early June, I'll plant summer maize right behind the combine. No time to plough — I'll seed directly into the stubble using hybrid seed, probably Denghai or Nongda. Maize is hungry but simple: one good application of compound fertilizer at sowing, two irrigations during jointing and grain filling, and three pesticide sprays for borers and weeds. I expect around 1200 jin per mu if the summer storms don't flatten it.

I thought about cotton or vegetables, but at my age I need crops I can sell without begging a buyer. The grain station takes wheat and corn no questions asked, and the government still pays a subsidy. That's worth more than a risky profit.
